title: Ain Jalut, 1260
hookLine: the Mamluks of Egypt stop the Mongol advance in Palestine

lines: A SPRING WITH AN OLD NAME.
cards: A letter arrives in Cairo from the Mongol camp. The chronicles say it demands surrender, with threats to match. Baghdad has fallen.
The cities of Syria have fallen or opened their gates. The sultan of Egypt, a soldier named Qutuz, has to answer. He could pay.

He could wait behind the walls and hope. Instead, the chronicles say, he marches his army north, out of Egypt, to meet them. The two armies come face to face beside a spring in Palestine, with a name out of an old story.

teach.b: Start with the name. 'Ayn is Arabic for a spring, and also for an eye. Jalut is the Qur'an's name for Goliath. So Ain Jalut is the spring of Goliath.
The Qur'an tells that story in surah al-Baqarah.

teach.h: TALUT, JALUT, AND A LITTLE COMPANY.
teach.b: A king called Talut, often identified with Saul, leads an army out against Jalut. He tests his men at a river: whoever drinks from it isn't with me, except one who scoops up a single handful. Most of them drink.
Only a few hold back. And that small group, facing Jalut's army, says, in Pickthall's English: "How many a little company hath overcome a mighty host by Allah's leave! Allah is with the steadfast."
They ask Allah for patience and firm feet. Then, the Qur'an says, David killed Goliath. Now the battle.

teach.h: THE MONGOLS STOPPED AT THE SPRING.
teach.b: The Mamluk army met the Mongols at that spring, and the Mamluks won. The Mongol advance toward Egypt stopped there. Among Qutuz's commanders was a man named Baybars.
And history doesn't end tidily: on the way home, the chronicles say, Qutuz was killed by his own officers, and Baybars became sultan. Why does the name matter?
Because, for the people who told this story, the place seemed to speak: a spring named for Goliath, where an army that had seemed unstoppable was stopped.
In this story, Allah is with the steadfast, the ones who hold their ground.
Holding your ground isn't the same as winning every fight. It means there's a line, and you stay on it.

how: Muslims read the story of Talut and Jalut in surah al-Baqarah, and its line that Allah is with the steadfast is often quoted in times of hardship.

o: the spring of Goliath, where the Mongols stopped
the hill outside Cairo where Qutuz waited
the river where Talut tested his soldiers

p: the king who tested his men at a river

s: Ain Jalut means the spring of Goliath
'ayn is a spring, and Jalut is the name the Qur'an gives Goliath.
in the Qur'an's story, most of Talut's men held back at the river
most drank. only a few held back, and they were the little company.
Qutuz ruled for many years after the battle
the chronicles say he was killed on the way home, and Baybars became sultan.

games.q: you're Qutuz, sultan in Cairo. a letter from the Mongol camp demands surrender, and city after city has fallen. what do you do?
o: pay, and keep Egypt safe for now.
games.why: the chronicles say he marched out of Egypt and met them at Ain Jalut, the spring of Goliath, and the Mamluks won.

practice: Put both feet flat on the floor and feel them there. Name, in a few words, one line in your life that keeps getting pushed, a habit, a yes you don't mean, a boundary, and picture the next test with your feet still on the ground.
If you pray, ask Allah for patience and firm feet, as the little company did; if not, simply hold the line in mind.

wordCard.voice: Ain Jalut. The spring of Goliath, in Palestine, where the Mamluks of Egypt stopped the Mongol advance. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the spring of Goliath. 'ayn is a spring or an eye; Jalut is the Qur'an's name for Goliath.

carryVoice: Your line: the spring of goliath. A little company, and steady feet on the ground. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: How many a little company hath overcome a mighty host by Allah's leave! Allah is with the steadfast.

sources.ref: Qur'an 2:246–251 (Talut, the river test, Jalut, David)
Mamluk-era chronicles, e.g. al-Maqrizi, al-Suluk (the letter, the march, the battle and Qutuz's death)
